When it occurs at bedtime, it's often mistaken for heart pain. Angina pectoris: This is a symptom of coronary artery disease that leads to reduced blood flowto the heart muscle. Painful episodes of angina can occur at rest or during physical activity. Anxiety: Chronic anxiety can lead to a sensation of discomfort in the chest region. Panic attacks canalso produce similar symptoms. Sleep apnea: Obstructive sleep apnoea is characterized by repeated interruptions in breathingduring sleep. In severe cases, people may awaken with a feeling of suffocation or chestpressure. Pulmonary embolism: A pulmonary em-bolus (blood clot) blocking an artery in your lung can decrease oxygen supply to the organand result in chest distress. Pneumonia: An infection of the lungs caused by bacteria, viruses or fungi can trigger chestpains. Depression: Some forms of depression can manifest physically as a persistent ache or discomfortin the torso area. If you frequently experience night chest discomforts, consult your physician to determine the underlyingcause and establish appropriate treatment options.

I am a nurse, so I can offer you some tips on managing your pain. First of all, check with your orthopedic surgeon to see if there is any reason why this pain could be related to an issue other than arthritis or wear and tear in your new knee joint. They may want to order x-rays or do some tests to rule out complications. If they feel that everything looks good, then here are some suggestions:
1) Exercise: Staying physically active helps to reduce pain and stiffness. You might consider low impact aerobic activities like walking, swimming, or cycling. Exercises that focus on range of motion also help increase flexibility around the joint and decrease pain (such as the quad stretch or using a foam roller on your quads). Always start slowly and build up over time.
 
2) Medications: Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) such as ibuprofen or naproxen can help manage the pain associated with arthritis. Discuss dosage and potential side effects with a healthcare provider. Acetaminophen may also be used to alleviate pain, but it does not have an antiinflammatory effect. Your surgeon may recommend a corticosteroid injection into the affected joint which can provide quick relief from inflammation and pain for several weeks at a time; however, these injections should only be done under medical supervision. 
 
3) Physical therapy: A physical therapist can create a customized exercise plan geared towards improving strength, balance, flexibility, and overall function. A PT will also teach you correct movement patterns to avoid aggravating the area. Physical therapists are trained to identify and address any limitations or muscle imbalances that may be contributing to your symptoms. 10 sessions of physical therapy may cost between $400 and $1,050 depending on the region. But this investment may well save money down the road by preventing more invasive treatments. 
 
4) Alternative therapies: There are other ways to manage knee pain besides medication and exercise. Some alternatives include acupuncture, massage therapy, cold laser therapy (low level light therapy), and transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS) units. These alternative therapies can often help relieve pain when used along with traditional treatment options. Talk with an acupuncturist or massage therapist about their methods for treating knee arthritis specifically. While these alternatives can be helpful, always discuss them with both your doctor and physical therapists first to make sure they're a safe and effective option for you. 5) Managing weight: Being overweight puts added stress on joints, including those in knees. Losing excess pounds can lessen pressure on arthritic joints and ease pain levels. Even modest weight loss can lead to significant improvement in knee function and comfort. However, try to be realistic with weight goals and give yourself time to achieve them.

what can I do ?
I'm sorry you are suffering so much. It is difficult to say without knowing more about your specific situation, but here are some things that may help:
1) Seek a second opinion from another pain management specialist or neurosurgeon. They may have a different perspective or recommend something different.
2) Ask your current doctor for a referral to a physical therapist knowledgeable in chronic and complex pain. Physical therapy can often be very helpful in managing pain, improving movement, and reducing medication usage. A physical therapists job is to help you find ways to move better and manage your pain through functional exercise. You dont want just any physical therapy, you need someone who understands your unique issues and challenges. Look for someone certified in orthopedic manual therapy (OMT), or a sports medicine PT, or someone with experience working with patients with chronic or complex needs. PTs can also teach you self-management techniques like trigger point therapy and myofascial release which can help with pain reduction. If you have access to an occupational therapist, they may also have some tools to offer. Occupational therapists focus on activities of daily living and helping people adapt to their pain/limitations. Sometimes OTs use adaptive equipment to support function or modify tasks. This can reduce strain and pain as well. An OT might also suggest an assistive device. There is a lot of overlap between OT and PT and sometimes both can contribute to your care. Also keep an eye out for any local pain support groups or community resources. Often these groups have people who have been through similar experiences and can share their knowledge. The National Pain Advocacy Network (NPAN) is also a good resource for finding information and support. 
3) Keep track of your symptoms, pain levels, what seems to work and what doesnt work. Keep a pain diary if you can. Record when the pain is worst, where it is felt, how intense it feels on a scale of 1-10, anything that helps relieve the symptoms (exercise, positions, etc.), and anything you think might be making it worse (like certain foods, activities, stressors, sleep). Recording this information can be really helpful because it allows you to see patterns and trends over time. From there you might start to identify triggers or factors that seem to exacerbate your condition. Once you recognize those, its easier to make lifestyle changes or ask your healthcare provider for adjustments. For example, if your diary shows you that eating spicy food makes your back pain worse, then you could talk to the doctor about modifying your diet or avoiding certain spices. Or if lying on your stomach makes the neck pain unbearable but lying in certain positions in bed helps alleviate it, maybe try using a pillow under your knees or shoulders to change up your positioning while sleeping. Knowing what works for you personally can empower you take control of some aspects of managing your chronic condition and reduce dependence on medication. Ultimately though, medication is there to treat pain not to solve all your problems. Your doctors will likely continue to adjust your medications based on what youre reporting and how effective they are. Be open and honest with them about whats going on and let them know what side effects youve experienced. Its important to remember that everyone heals at a differently paced and managed by different treatments. Dont compare yourself to others or feel like you should be doing better than someone else. Everyone's journey is different and your timeline is not up to you, nor is it up the doctors. Perseverance and patience are key. Know that you're not alone in this fight and that there are many resources available to assist you along the way.

Pollution & Irritants: Air pollution, cigarette smoke, chemicals, dust mites, etc. can irritate sinusal passages leading to congestion and inflammation. Nasal Polyps: These noncancerous growths develop in the sinusable passages causing blockage and difficulty in breathing. In some cases, they can recur despite treatment. Infections: Bacterial, viral, fungal, parasitic infections can lead to chronic inflammation of sinuss. Head trauma: Severe head trauma can damage sinuous passages resulting in blockages and fluid build up. Medical Conditions: Certain medical conditions like Diabetes, Celiac disease, Sjogren s syndrome can increase the risk for chronic Rhinosinusis. How to treat chronic Sinus It is recommended to consult an ENT specialist who will diagnose the underlying cause and recommend appropriate treatment plan based on your specific condition. There are several treatments options available including medications (antihistamines, decongestants, corticosteroids), sinuscircumscrition, surgery, lifestyle modifications, avoiding allergens & irritants. When you consume large amounts of caffeine over a short period of time, your body becomes dependent on the caffeine to function normally. Then, when you suddenly stop consuming caffeine or reduce the amount consumed, you experience withdrawal effects because your brain and body have become used to having caffeine around.
Symptoms can include fatigue, weakness, headaches, nausea, irritability, dizziness, and tremors. The severity of these symptoms can vary from person to person, depending on how much caffeine was consumed previously and individual tolerance levels. Withdrawal symptoms usually begin within 6-12 hours of the last dose of coffee, tea, cola, or other sources of stimulants containing caffeine, peak between 24-48 hours, then gradually subside as the body adjusts to the absence of additional caffeine intake.
